title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is finding the natural frequencies of a uniform elastic lamina clamped at x=a and free at x=0, i.e. a cantilever. He uses the separated solution y = (A cos θx/b + B sin θx/b + C e^{θx/b} + D e^{-θx/b}) · sin/cos(θ²t). The free end gives two conditions, y''=0 and y'''=0, so A=C+D and B=C-D. The clamped end gives y=0 and y'=0. Requiring a nonzero solution (C/D computed in two ways) produces the frequency equation 2 = -cos Φ (e^Φ + e^{-Φ}), with Φ = θa/b. In modern form this is 1 + cos Φ cosh Φ = 0, the classical clamped-free Euler–Bernoulli beam characteristic equation.

On this page Euler first notes the vibration time. Taking one 'vibration' to end when θ²t = π gives a time of π/θ². This is a half-period, the usual 18th-century convention for a 'vibration'.

He then locates the roots qualitatively. Set ρ = π/2. For Φ = ρ+ω, 3ρ-ω, 5ρ+ω, 7ρ-ω, 9ρ+ω, … one has -cos Φ = sin ω in every case. The equation therefore becomes 2 = sin ω · (e^{(2n-1)ρ ± ω} + e^{-(2n-1)ρ ∓ ω}). Because the exponential factor grows rapidly, ω is small and keeps decreasing. So the roots lie alternately just above and just below the odd multiples of π/2. Negative roots are just the mirror images, since the equation is even in Φ.

On the next page he expands in series and obtains the first root ω ≈ 0.30432, Φ ≈ 1.87511.

Modern restatement: the roots β_n of cos β cosh β = -1 satisfy β_n ≈ (2n-1)π/2 + (-1)^{n+1}·2e^{-(2n-1)π/2}. Euler's alternation pattern is exactly this asymptotic structure. The values are 1.8751, 4.6941, 7.8548, …
errors: The running text says 'alternatim minores et maiores quam 5ρ, 7ρ, 11ρ etc.', skipping 9ρ. The table that follows correctly uses 9ρ, so '11ρ' is a misprint for '9ρ'.

This is not an error, but note the convention: 'tempus vnius vibrationis' = π/θ² is a half-period of the factor cos θ²t (the full period is 2π/θ²). This matches the period-counting convention of the time.
The table is correct. For each case one can check that cos((2n-1)π/2 ± ω) = -sin ω, with the sign of ω chosen so that the leading term is the positive large exponential.

ideas.what: Frequency equation of the clamped-free elastic beam, 1 + cos Φ cosh Φ = 0
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Daniel Bernoulli (1730s–1744); Euler, Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I (1744)
ideas.where_published: Euler, Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (1744), Additamentum I; Euler's earlier vibration papers; reviewed in Truesdell's history of rational mechanics of flexible/elastic bodies (Opera omnia II.11)

ideas.what: Root localization: roots lie alternately just above and below the odd multiples of π/2, with corrections ω decreasing to 0
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (qualitatively), later standard (e.g. Rayleigh, Theory of Sound)
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (1744), Additamentum I, and this paper E443

ideas.what: Substitution Φ = (2n-1)ρ ± ω, turning -cos Φ into sin ω to set up small-ω series solution
ideas.modern_name: Perturbative root-finding near the asymptotic zeros
ideas.where_published: E443 and Euler's numerical-analysis practice generally

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine re-derivation and root localization of the well-known cantilever frequency equation, which Euler had already treated in 1744 and which is thoroughly documented by Truesdell. The only oddity is a misprint (11ρ for 9ρ).
transcription_corrections: The smudged word 'In positi[..]' should read 'In positiuis'.
The printed text indeed reads '5ρ, 7ρ, 11ρ'. The transcription is faithful, but the mathematics requires '9ρ'.
In table line V the print renders the exponent like 'e^{sρ}e^{+ω}'; it is e^{9ρ}e^{+ω}, as transcribed.
